title: Wrapped bar
subtitle: Overcast bars that finish the remaining threads after hardanger cutting
excerpt: A wrapped bar is worked after threads have been cut and withdrawn from a hardanger design, leaving groups of fabric threads exposed across open squares. The working thread is wound tightly around each group in close, even wraps from one end to the other. The result is a firm, smooth bar with a neat cord-like surface.
sourceNotes: Standard hardanger withdrawn-thread technique; documented in Elsie Svennas, A Handbook of Hardanger Embroidery (1977) and in general counted-thread needlework references.

content.text: Once the threads inside a hardanger square have been cut and withdrawn, what remains is a set of parallel fabric threads spanning the open space. A wrapped bar covers one group of those threads by winding the working thread around them in tight, even coils. The bar must be firm enough to hold its shape without puckering the surrounding fabric.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Perle cotton no 8 for bars and fillings; no 5 was used for the kloster blocks

items.label: Fabric
items.value: 28-count evenweave linen or 22-count hardanger fabric, with kloster blocks already complete and threads cut

items.label: Scissors
items.value: Small sharp scissors for trimming thread ends

content.text: Before starting any bars, confirm that all
bordering each square are complete. Cut and withdraw the threads running parallel to the blocks' stitches, leaving only the threads that run perpendicular. These perpendicular threads form the bars.
Secure the working thread by running the needle under the back of a nearby kloster block. Bring the needle up at the base of the first bar, at the edge of the fabric where the block ends.

Pass the needle under the bar threads from right to left, then bring the working thread over the top of the bar and under again. Pull each wrap firmly so it sits close against the previous one. Work every wrap in the same direction so the bar has a consistent twist. Cover the entire length of the bar from one kloster block edge to the other with no gaps.

At the far end, slide the needle under the nearest kloster block on the back to travel to the next bar. Repeat the wrapping process. The wraps on every bar in the design should face the same way and be the same tightness.
When all bars are wrapped, secure the thread end under the blocks on the back. Trim neatly. The bars should lie flat and taut across the open squares.

items.symptom: Wraps are uneven or loose in places
items.cause: Tension on the working thread varied during wrapping, or the wraps were not kept parallel
items.fix: Pull each wrap with the same firm tension before placing the next. Keep the working thread at a consistent angle as you wind.

items.symptom: The bar puckers or the fabric around it pulls
items.cause: The working thread is too thick for the scale of the work, or the wraps are too tight at the bar ends
items.fix: Use perle no 8 rather than no 5 for bars. Ease the tension slightly at the very start and end of each bar where it meets the kloster block.

items.symptom: Threads were cut before all blocks were finished
items.cause: The safety order was not followed
items.fix: This cannot be undone cleanly. In future work, always complete every kloster block in the design before cutting a single thread. Mark cut areas with a pin as a reminder.
